name: Synthetic Portraiture
title: Synthetic Portraiture
answer: Synthetic portraiture is the creation of photographic or hyper-realistic images of human faces and figures that do not depict a real person. It sits at the boundary between photography and digital painting, producing work that can be indistinguishable from a studio portrait while originating entirely from algorithmic generation. The practice includes both fully invented faces and the stylized or altered rendering of existing likenesses, and it is used in editorial, advertising, fine art, and identity prototyping.

It sits at the boundary between photography and digital painting, producing work that can be indistinguishable from a studio portrait while originating entirely from algorithmic generation. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard GPU-accelerated computers, either locally or through cloud services, using generative models trained on large datasets of photographs and paintings. Training a model from scratch requires substantial compute and curated data, but most practitioners use pre-trained checkpoints and fine-tune them on smaller, targeted sets of portraits. Inference for a single high-resolution image can run on a consumer graphics card, though batch production and video-style animation demand more memory and faster hardware.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A portrait is typically produced by prompting a text-to-image model or by blending and inpainting within a latent space, then refining the result through repeated sampling and manual adjustment. Artists control composition, lighting, skin texture, and expression through prompt wording, negative prompts, and reference images, often moving between generative passes and traditional retouching tools. The goal is not a single lucky output but a controlled workflow where the model proposes variations and the artist selects and corrects them toward a finished likeness.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main rights questions concern training data, likeness, and disclosure. A synthetic portrait may be built from photographs of real people without consent, and even an invented face can closely resemble a living person, raising privacy and publicity concerns. Provenance is often unclear because generated files do not carry a reliable record of their sources or edits, and many jurisdictions have not settled whether a purely synthetic portrait attracts copyright at all. Practitioners should document their prompts, seeds, and source images, and avoid presenting a synthetic portrait as a photograph of a real, identifiable person without clear labeling.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real-time generation, controllable identity consistency, and tighter integration with traditional photography pipelines. As models improve at preserving a fixed face across many images, synthetic portraiture will support virtual actors, product avatars, and historical reconstruction with less manual cleanup. At the same time, detection and provenance standards are likely to become a normal part of professional practice, so that a synthetic portrait can be verified as synthetic and traced to its creator.
